evidence.title: How the EU's Carbon Border Tax is Reshaping Indian MSMEs (The Wire)
evidence.quote: A fastener and steel products exporter, a typical Indian MSME, was informed by its customers in Denmark and Germany that Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) reports had become mandatory. Lacking any in-house capacity to comply, the firm hired a consultant at an annual cost of nearly Rs 2 lakh.
evidence.statement: An Indian fastener MSME told by Danish and German customers that CBAM reports were mandatory hired a consultant for about Rs 2 lakh a year.

evidence.title: How the EU's Carbon Border Tax is Reshaping Indian MSMEs (The Wire)
evidence.quote: The company has since received compliance warnings and reported losing orders.
evidence.statement: The same exporter received compliance warnings and reported losing orders.

evidence.title: How the EU's Carbon Border Tax is Reshaping Indian MSMEs (The Wire)
evidence.quote: IamSMEofIndia’s survey found that 35% of member firms had already received requests for emissions-related data, either directly from European customers or through Indian firms supplying European markets. Yet none reported receiving any assistance from buyers in understanding CBAM requirements or building compliance capacity.
evidence.statement: In an MSME association survey, 35% of firms had received emissions-data requests, and none had received help from buyers, which argues against buyers sponsoring supplier packs.

evidence.title: How the EU's Carbon Border Tax is Reshaping Indian MSMEs (The Wire)
evidence.quote: According to his firm’s survey, 41% of responding firms have invested in solar power or energy-efficient equipment over the past two years. Yet only 24% measure their emissions.
evidence.statement: Only 24% of surveyed MSMEs measure their emissions.

evidence.title: How the EU's Carbon Border Tax is Reshaping Indian MSMEs (The Wire)
evidence.quote: A typical exporter often sources components from dozens of small vendors, many of whom do not have machine-level energy meters or systems to measure emissions.
evidence.statement: Exporters' many small vendors often lack meters or systems to measure emissions.

evidence.title: How the EU's Carbon Border Tax is Reshaping Indian MSMEs (The Wire)
evidence.quote: While welcoming the Union government’s proposal to bear up to 90% of MSME compliance costs

summary.statement: Exporters typically hire consultants (about Rs 2 lakh a year in one case) or spend months with experts; few measure emissions (24%).
Data must come from many small vendors and utilities that lack meters or don't respond.
Fastener importers collect data through the free EFDA template and their own supplier portals, but only 12% of suppliers returned specific values.
35% of surveyed MSMEs had received emissions-data requests from EU customers or intermediaries.
Importers may now declare on defaults without collecting actual data, and importers under 50 tonnes a year are exempt, so many small buyers may never ask.
No source measures how often buyers specifically ask for verified actual data rather than any data.
Reported costs range from about Rs 2 lakh a year for a consultant to Rs 10 lakh for certification and Rs 5-10 million for full compliance.
A proposed government scheme would reimburse up to 90% of certification and verification costs for micro and small exporters.
Verification capacity is scarce: no accredited CBAM verifier was listed as of October 2026.
On defaults, importers price the worst case and push it back onto suppliers through price cuts (15-22% estimated) or lost orders; small EU buyers have disappeared for some exporters.
EU distributors are starting to select suppliers able to provide emissions data.
For coal-based Indian steel routes, defaults are close to real emissions, so verified data may save little.
No public evidence on who approves compliance purchases inside small exporters; needs interviews.
Exporters use consultants and Indian CBAM vendors (CleanCarbon.ai, The Sustainability Cloud, GreenSutra); importers use CBAMBOO and portals.
Free tools already cover the decision step: GreenSutra's default-vs-verified calculator and the EFDA calculator.
The export-promotion channel is already taken: SEPC launched a CBAM platform with CleanCarbon.ai.
Consultants are often still learning and hard to reach outside major centres.

new_unknowns.question: For the target products and input routes (e.g. coal-based DRI or induction-furnace steel), how often is verified actual data meaningfully below the default?
What would an exporter pay for a decision pack when GreenSutra's calculator is free and 90% of verification may be reimbursed?
What share of EU buyers of small Indian exporters import over 50 tonnes a year and so need CBAM data at all?
